got_right: Randomizing headline type produced large, precise effects: misinformation −18.2 points (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks −13.3 points on sharing, against a 60.3% baseline for true or neutral headlines. Both are well above the MDE of about 0.031.

The report is candid that the six sharer attributes are measured traits of real contacts, so their contrasts are descriptive rather than causal. It also re-weights by inverse assignment probability, which leaves the close-tie and high-trust results intact (R: +3.0 and +6.7 points).

Collecting both sharing and plausibility for each profile, with a registered plan and registered moderators, allows a direct test of whether the two diverge. The E1 comparison shows they largely do not (−18.2 vs −18.6).

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The sharer features are respondents' own ratings of real contacts, so trust, tie, ideology and knowledge are bundled and confounded. The study cannot say whether source attributes matter causally, which is the 'who shares what from whom' premise in the title.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Design section: only information type is randomized. The tie contrast of +3.0 points and the high-trust contrast of +5.7 points are labelled descriptive.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The low-trust, low-knowledge and foreign-origin reference groups are small, so the null results for the sharer attributes are weakly informative. Even naive MDEs exceed plausible effects, and they ignore clustering.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: The Trust: low reference has n=828 and an MDE of 0.051–0.056. The observed mid-trust effect of 0.036 has p=0.056. The MDE for origin is 0.032, against an observed 0.002.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Sharing and plausibility are both forced-choice picks between two profiles. The two outcomes are nearly identical, so the study cannot separate sharing from believing. Sharing is stated, not behavioural.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Misinformation effect of −0.182 on sharing vs −0.186 on plausibility. Per-model N is about 11,880.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Respondents' own belief in disputed claims and their media trust flip the misinformation effect, but sharer attributes do not interact with these moderators. The moderator results are many uncorrected subgroup contrasts, so they are exploratory.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: S3: highest minus lowest tertile of belief in disputed claims +5.6 points for misinformation (p<0.001) and −5.5 points for true or neutral headlines. S4: +4.8 points for misinformation with high media trust.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The sample is US Latino YouGov panelists only. The language split shows the misinformation penalty differs (English −20.1 vs Spanish −14.4), so the headline result may not carry to other populations.

debates.label: Is sharing misinformation driven by belief?
debates.position_a: Sharing tracks perceived plausibility, so susceptibility to misinformation is a belief problem and corrections should target accuracy.
debates.position_b: Sharing and belief come apart depending on who the source is and on group or identity motives, so conspiracy-prone sharers or people may spread claims regardless of plausibility.
debates.what_this_study_says: Leans to position A on average, since the share and plausibility effects are nearly identical. Because both outcomes are forced choices and the sharer attributes are not randomized, it cannot test whether source attributes pull sharing away from plausibility. Respondents' belief in disputed claims raises misinformation sharing and plausibility alike (S3 and S8).

briefs.title: Randomized source cues and separate sharing and belief measures
briefs.question: Do randomly assigned source trust and tie strength change willingness to share a false headline more than they change its perceived accuracy?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Fixes the design and measurement causes. Randomizing source cues turns the descriptive trust and tie contrasts into causal effects. Rating sharing and accuracy separately on 1–7 scales lets the two outcomes diverge.
briefs.design_sketch: Respondents see a single headline (true, false or fact-check) attributed to a fictional contact, with tie (close or distant) and trust (high or low) randomized, which gives a 3×2×2 factorial. Each respondent rates sharing intent and perceived accuracy on separate scales, and a subsample makes a real, incentivized share-or-not choice. Recruit US Latino YouGov adults, stratified by survey language.

power_target.basis: Observed trust effect of 0.057 (H5) and MDE of 0.051 for Trust: high vs Trust: low. About 1,000 per cell gives an MDE near 0.05 on a 0/1 outcome; closer to 1,300 per cell is needed for the tie effect of 0.03 under clustering.

briefs.title: Belief-driven versus identity-driven sharing of misinformation
briefs.question: Does sharing of a false claim follow its perceived plausibility, or does it vary with source ideology independently of plausibility?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Fixes the missing_moderator and design causes. Randomizing source ideology and measuring both outcomes lets sharing diverge from belief when sources are co-partisan, which the original could not test.
briefs.design_sketch: Show a false or true headline from a randomized source (co-ideological, opposed, or neutral) to respondents classified by their own ideology and belief in disputed claims. Measure accuracy judgements and sharing intent on separate scales, and test the interaction of source ideology with outcome in a within-subject design. If sharing follows belief, the source effect on both outcomes is the same; if identity drives sharing, the source effect on sharing exceeds its effect on accuracy.

power_target.basis: Moderator contrasts of about 0.055 (S3) with SEs near 0.017; the sharer ideology effect of 0.019 (H4) is smaller, so a cell of 1,500 targets an interaction MDE near 0.04.

briefs.title: Replication across populations and languages
briefs.question: Does the misinformation sharing penalty and the source-trust gradient hold in non-Latino and in Spanish- versus English-language samples?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Fixes the sample cause. The original shows a smaller penalty among Spanish-language respondents (−14.4 vs −20.1), but only within a Latino sample.
briefs.design_sketch: Run the same conjoint with the same randomized headline type on matched YouGov samples of white, Black and Latino adults, with Latino respondents split by survey language. Keep the outcomes and registered moderators unchanged. Test whether the information-type effect varies by group and language.

power_target.basis: The language gap is 0.057 (−0.201 vs −0.144), with SEs near 0.014–0.020. About 1,500 per group-by-arm cell gives an MDE near 0.04.

verdict: A follow-up is worth running. The headline result is solid: misinformation is shared and believed about 18 points less, and the study's main gap is causal inference about sources, since every sharer attribute was measured rather than assigned. Run Randomized source cues and separate sharing and belief measures first. It randomizes trust and tie, which carried the only notable sharer signals (+5.7 and +3.0 points), and it separates sharing from belief, which the forced-choice outcomes here conflate. The belief-versus-identity design comes second and the cross-population replication third.
